definition: A small, sturdy four-wheel-drive vehicle, originally developed for military use.
origin: Jeep most likely derives from "GP," a US Army abbreviation for "general purpose" vehicle, though the exact origin is debated, and some trace it instead to Eugene the Jeep, a mysterious, all-capable creature in the 1930s Popeye comic strip, whose can-do reputation made soldiers apply his name to their versatile new vehicle. The rugged military vehicle built for the Second World War kept the nickname permanently, and Jeep later became a registered trademark.

definition: A brand name, used generically, for an inexpensive, easy-to-use camera.
origin: Kodak is not named after a person at all, but was deliberately invented from nothing by George Eastman (1854–1932), founder of the Eastman Kodak Company, who wanted a short, strong, easily pronounced word starting and ending with his favourite letter, "K," with no meaning in any language to trip up trademark disputes. The resulting invented brand name became so dominant in consumer photography that it entered everyday speech as shorthand for any simple snapshot camera.

definition: A concave plastic disc thrown between players as a game or sport.
origin: Frisbee is named after the Frisbie Pie Company of Bridgeport, Connecticut, whose empty metal pie tins, stamped with the bakery's name, were tossed by nearby college students for fun in the early twentieth century. When Walter Morrison later developed a plastic version of the flying disc in the 1950s, the toy company Wham-O bought his design, altered the spelling, and named it Frisbee in honour of the pie tins that started the game.

definition: A durable floor covering made from a hardened mixture of linseed oil, cork dust, and other materials on a canvas backing.
origin: Linoleum is not a personal eponym but a deliberate scientific coinage by its 1863 inventor, Frederick Walton, from Latin linum (flax, the source of linseed oil) and oleum (oil). Walton patented the durable, affordable flooring material and built an entire industry around it, though the word itself, rather than his name, is what survived into everyday use, eventually shortened informally to "lino."

definition: A trademark for a soft, translucent petroleum jelly used as a skin moisturiser and protectant.
origin: Vaseline is a deliberately coined brand name invented in 1872 by Robert Chesebrough, an American chemist who had noticed oil rig workers using a waxy residue that formed on drilling equipment to heal cuts and burns. He refined the substance into petroleum jelly and built the word from German Wasser (water) and Greek elaion (olive oil), producing a brand name so successful it became genericised for petroleum jelly of any make.

definition: A trademark for a bath or pool fitted with underwater jets that massage the body with swirling water.
origin: Jacuzzi is named after the Jacuzzi family, Italian immigrants to California who ran a machine shop making aircraft propellers and irrigation pumps. In 1956, brother Candido Jacuzzi designed a portable underwater pump to ease the pain of his young son's arthritis by giving him hydrotherapy at home, and the family later adapted the invention into the built-in whirlpool bath that carries their surname worldwide.

definition: A trademark for a hard, durable, heat-resistant laminate used for kitchen worktops and furniture surfaces.
origin: Formica was invented in 1912 by Daniel O'Conor and Herbert Faber, American engineers who developed a laminate to replace mica, a natural mineral then used as electrical insulation, coining the brand name to mean literally "for mica," its intended substitute. The material later proved ideal for durable, easy-to-clean kitchen surfaces, and the brand name became a generic word for laminate worktops in general.

definition: A fastening device consisting of two rows of interlocking teeth closed or opened by a sliding tab.
origin: Zipper takes its name not from an inventor but from a 1923 marketing decision: the B.F. Goodrich Company used an improved sliding fastener, based on earlier designs by Whitcomb Judson and Gideon Sundback, on a new line of rubber boots, and named the boots "Zippers" for the brisk "zip" sound the fastener made when pulled. The catchy sound-word for the boots soon transferred to the fastener itself, and it stuck permanently.
